lede: Real tables grow every day, and jobs get rerun. Partitioned folders let a reader skip the days it doesn't need, and the write mode decides whether a rerun replaces data, adds to it or doubles it.
objectives: Write a table split into folders by a column with `partitionBy`
Read a partitioned folder back, whole or one partition at a time
Choose between the `overwrite`, `append`, `ignore` and `error` write modes
Replace only the partitions a write touches with dynamic partition overwrite

blocks.md:
`observations` holds weather readings from four stations over two days. `observation_date` is the UTC date of each reading, and it's the natural column to split the files by: most questions ask about particular days.

`df.write.partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)` writes one sub-folder per value, named `column=value`, and puts each row in its value's folder. The column itself isn't stored inside the files: its value lives in the folder name. The examples list the folders with plain Python's `os.listdir`, sorted, and leave out the files, whose names change on every run.

blocks.title: One folder per day
blocks.note: Two days, two folders. Every reading from 7 March is in the first and every reading from 8 March in the second.

blocks.md:
Reading the top folder gives the whole table back. Spark finds the `column=value` folders, adds the partition column back, and works out its type from the values, here a `date`. It's added as the **last** column.

A query that asks for one day only needs one folder, so Spark can skip the rest without opening them. You can also point a read straight at one partition's folder. Then the partition column isn't there, because it's not in the files; the `basePath` option tells Spark where the table starts, so it adds the column back.

blocks.title: Read all of it, or one day
blocks.code:
observations.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet("/tmp/weather/obs")

whole = spark.read.parquet("/tmp/weather/obs")
print(whole.columns)
print(dict(whole.dtypes)["observation_date"], whole.count())

day = spark.read.parquet("/tmp/weather/obs/observation_date=2026-03-08")
print(day.count(), day.columns[-1])

day = spark.read.option("basePath", "/tmp/weather/obs").parquet("/tmp/weather/obs/observation_date=2026-03-08")
print(day.count(), day.columns[-1])
blocks.note: `observation_date` has moved to the end, typed as a date. The 8 March folder holds 7 readings; read on its own it has no date column, and with `basePath` it has it again.

blocks.md: Partition by a column with **few distinct values** that queries often pick out: a date, a country, a status. Partitioning by something like `observation_id` would make one tiny folder per row. You can give several columns; each becomes a level of folders.

blocks.title: Two levels of folders
blocks.note: Each day folder has one folder per station that reported that day. NYC-01 only reported on 8 March, so it appears only there.

blocks.md:
The write **mode** decides what happens when the path already exists:

- `error` (also `errorifexists`, the default) refuses and raises an error.
- `overwrite` deletes what's there and writes the new data.
- `append` adds new files next to the old ones. Run the same append twice and every row is there twice.
- `ignore` does nothing at all if the path exists.

blocks.title: Append, ignore and overwrite
blocks.code:
path = "/tmp/weather/modes"
observations.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print("overwrite:", spark.read.parquet(path).count())

observations.write.mode("append").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print("append:   ", spark.read.parquet(path).count())

observations.write.mode("ignore").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print("ignore:   ", spark.read.parquet(path).count())

observations.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print("overwrite:", spark.read.parquet(path).count())
blocks.note: Appending the same 12 readings again gives 24: nothing checks for repeats. `ignore` left the folder alone. `overwrite` put it back to 12, which is why a job that may be rerun usually overwrites.

blocks.md: A plain `overwrite` replaces the **whole** folder, every partition, even when the new data covers only one day. To fix one day, that's a disaster. With the option `partitionOverwriteMode` set to `dynamic`, an overwrite replaces only the partitions that appear in the new data and leaves the others alone.

blocks.title: Replace just one day
blocks.code:
import os


def folders(path):
    return sorted(d for d in os.listdir(path) if "=" in d)

from datetime import date, datetime

fix = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("OBS-000012", "NYC-01", datetime(2026, 3, 8, 8, 0), date(2026, 3, 8), 0.7, 77, 0.4, 12.9, 1015.3, "estimated")],
    observations.schema,
)

path = "/tmp/weather/fixes"
observations.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)

fix.write.mode("overwrite").option("partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print(folders(path), spark.read.parquet(path).count())

fix.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("observation_date").parquet(path)
print(folders(path), spark.read.parquet(path).count())
blocks.note: `fix` is one corrected reading for 8 March. The dynamic overwrite replaced the 8 March folder with it and kept 7 March: 5 + 1 = 6 readings. The plain overwrite wiped both days and left just the one reading.

blocks.title: Partitioning by a column that isn't there
blocks.note: The column is `observation_date`, and Spark checks before writing anything. The error lists the columns the DataFrame does have.

concept.prompt: You write with `partitionBy("observation_date")` and read the top folder back. Where is `observation_date`?
choices: Missing: it's only in the folder names
Back, as the last column, with its type worked out from the folder names
concept.why: Spark rebuilds the column from the `column=value` folders and adds it at the end; it infers a date from values like 2026-03-08.

concept.prompt: A job appends the same day's readings twice by mistake. What happens?
choices: The second append replaces the first
Every reading of that day is stored twice
concept.why: `append` adds new files without looking at what's there, so the rows are duplicated. A rerunnable job overwrites.

concept.prompt: A folder holds 14 days. You overwrite it with one corrected day, with `partitionOverwriteMode` set to `dynamic`. What's left?
choices: All 14 days, with the corrected day replaced
concept.why: Dynamic overwrite replaces only the partitions present in the new data. A plain overwrite would leave only the corrected day.

review: `write.partitionBy("col")` makes one `col=value` folder per value; the value lives in the folder name, not the files.
Reading the top folder adds the partition column back, last, with an inferred type. Queries for some values can skip the other folders.
Reading one partition's folder drops the column unless you set `basePath`.
Partition by a column with few values that queries pick out, such as a date.
Modes: `error` (default) refuses, `overwrite` replaces, `append` adds (and duplicates on a rerun), `ignore` does nothing if the path exists.
`option("partitionOverwriteMode", "dynamic")` overwrites only the partitions in the new data.
